_about: Published classifications the Find your method tree can be viewed through, one at a time. question: schemes for the left side (what you study), mapping each kind of question (suit). tool: schemes for the right side (your tool), mapping each Method (design id). In each scheme, items maps an id to the group(s) it belongs to; basis says how: named (the source itself names it) or definition (we applied the source's own definition, see note). An id left out of items is not classified by that source, and the app shows it as such. The first scheme on each side is the game's own grouping, labelled as ours. How each source was checked: docs/method-tree-sources.md, docs/method-tree-taxonomies.md, docs/method-tree-mesh.md.

question.name: The game's suits
question.cite: Methodical's own nine kinds of question (the suits on the cards).

question.name: Saunders et al. (2019)
question.cite: Saunders, Lewis & Thornhill (2019). Research Methods for Business Students, section 5.7, pp. 186–188. Pearson.

groups.name: Exploratory
groups.def: Ask open questions to discover what is happening.

groups.name: Descriptive
groups.def: Gain an accurate profile of events, persons or situations.

groups.name: Explanatory
groups.def: Establish causal relationships between variables.

groups.name: Evaluative
groups.def: Find out how well something works.

ASSOCIATE.note: The book's own example of explanatory research is a correlation (scrap rates and machine age).

CAUSE.note: Causal relationships are explanatory; the effectiveness of a policy or programme is evaluative.

EXPLAIN.note: Explanatory questions ask why or how.

MEASURE.note: How well a test or instrument works.

question.name: Gregor (2006)
question.what: Goals of theory: what a study's answer is for
question.cite: Gregor (2006). The Nature of Theory in Information Systems. MIS Quarterly 30(3), Table 2, p. 620.

groups.name: Analysis
groups.def: Says what is.

groups.name: Explanation
groups.def: Says what is, how, why, when, and where.

groups.name: Prediction
groups.def: Says what is and what will be.

groups.name: Explanation and prediction
groups.def: Causal explanations and testable propositions.

groups.name: Design and action
groups.def: Says how to do something.

DESCRIBE.note: Gregor's first goal is analysis and description.

EXPLORE.note: Describing what is going on, without testing causes.

MEASURE.note: Defining and describing the constructs themselves.

EXPLAIN.note: How and why, from a mechanism or theory.

tool.name: The game's families
tool.cite: Methodical's own nine Method families (the colours on the cards). Each says below which published category it follows, if any.

descriptive.cite: Grimes & Schulz (2002): observational studies without a comparison group are descriptive.
descriptive.note: Grimes & Schulz and MeSH count cross-sectional studies as analytical; the game files them here.

analytical.cite: Grimes & Schulz (2002): observational studies with a comparison group are analytical.

quasi.cite: Own grouping. The term follows the ERIC thesaurus descriptor "Quasiexperimental Design".
quasi.note: No family of its own in Grimes & Schulz, MeSH or EQUATOR.

experimental.cite: Grimes & Schulz (2002): the investigator assigns the exposure.

qualitative.note: Mixed methods has no MeSH heading.

synthesis.cite: MeSH 2026: Evidence Synthesis (D000099290, publication type V03.500).
synthesis.note: MeSH files bibliometric methods (co-citation, coupling) under information science.

measurement.cite: MeSH 2026: Validation Study (D023361); otherwise the game's own grouping.

computational.cite: Own grouping: no published category groups models, simulation, prediction and cost-effectiveness.

engineering.cite: Own grouping, anchored in Hevner et al. (2004), design science, and Gregor (2006), design and action.

tool.name: Grimes & Schulz (2002)
tool.cite: Grimes & Schulz (2002). An overview of clinical research: the lay of the land. Lancet 359: 57–61.
tool.rule: Did the investigator assign the exposure? Yes: experimental. No: observational, which is analytical if it has a comparison group and descriptive if not.

groups.name: Experimental
groups.def: The investigator assigns the exposure.

groups.name: Observational, analytical
groups.def: Not assigned by the investigator; has a comparison group.

groups.name: Observational, descriptive
groups.def: Not assigned by the investigator; no comparison group.

rct.note: Randomised trials are the experimental studies the overview names.

cluster-rct.note: The investigator assigns the exposure, by group.

crossover.note: The investigator assigns the order of exposures.

n-of-1.note: The investigator assigns treatments within one person.

stepped-wedge.note: The investigator assigns when each group starts.

ab-test.note: The investigator assigns users to versions.

adaptive-platform.note: The investigator assigns patients to arms.

field-experiment.note: The investigator assigns the treatment in the field.

pdsa.note: The team assigns the change, without randomisation: a non-randomised experiment.

cohort-prospective.note: Cohort studies are named among the analytical studies.

cohort-retrospective.note: Cohort studies are named among the analytical studies.

cross-sectional.note: Named as analytical here; the game files it as descriptive.

case-crossover.note: Each case is compared with itself at an earlier time.

case-cohort.note: Cases are compared with a sample of the cohort.

target-trial.note: Observational data, compared as in a trial.

iv.note: Observational; groups compared by an instrument.

gwas.note: Observational; people with and without the trait are compared.

did.note: Not assigned by the investigator; an untreated comparison group.

rdd.note: Assigned by a rule, not the investigator; compared across the cutoff.

its.note: Not assigned by the investigator; compared before and after.

synthetic-control.note: Not assigned by the investigator; compared with a built comparison unit.

case-report.note: Case series are the overview's example of a descriptive study.

surveillance.note: Counts and trends, without a comparison group.

capture-recapture.note: Estimates a population's size, without a comparison group.

tool.name: MeSH 2026
tool.what: Study designs and methods in the U.S. National Library of Medicine's subject headings
tool.cite: U.S. National Library of Medicine. Medical Subject Headings (MeSH), 2026 edition, checked through the MeSH RDF API on 2026-11-17.
tool.rule: Each Method sits under the MeSH heading that names it, grouped by the MeSH tree; where MeSH has no heading for it, under the nearest broader one, or not classified.

case-cohort.note: Case-Control Studies (D016022). 'Nested Case-Control Studies' is an entry term of Case-Control Studies; case-cohort itself has no term.

did.note: Controlled Before-After Studies (D065187). Controlled Before-After Studies is the design that difference-in-differences analyses.

rdd.note: Non-Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic (D065228). No heading; 'Quasi-Experimental Studies' is an entry term of Non-Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic.

its.note: Interrupted Time Series Analysis (D065186). Own heading, under Epidemiologic Studies.

synthetic-control.note: Non-Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic (D065228). No heading; nearest is Non-Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic (entry term Quasi-Experimental Studies). Doubtful.

rct.note: Randomized Controlled Trial (D016449). Publication type, under Controlled Clinical Trial.

cluster-rct.note: Randomized Controlled Trial (D016449). No heading or entry term for cluster randomization; nearest is Randomized Controlled Trial.

crossover.note: Cross-Over Studies (D018592). Own heading, but MeSH files it under Epidemiologic Research Design, not under Clinical Trial.

stepped-wedge.note: Randomized Controlled Trial (D016449). No heading or entry term; nearest is Randomized Controlled Trial.

grounded-theory.note: Grounded Theory (D066296). Own heading, under Empirical Research beside Qualitative Research.

mixed-sequential.note: Empirical Research (D036262). No heading or entry term for mixed methods; nearest heading covering both strands is Empirical Research.

systematic-review.note: Systematic Review (D000078182). Publication type under Evidence Synthesis; Meta-Analysis is its sibling.

scoping-review.note: Scoping Review (D000098583). Publication type under Evidence Synthesis.

network-meta.note: Network Meta-Analysis (D000099094). Only tree V03.600.001 under Meta-Analysis, which is also V03.500.004; grouped through that parent.

ipd-meta.note: Meta-Analysis (D017418). No heading for individual participant data; nearest is Meta-Analysis (V03.500.004).

umbrella-review.note: Systematic Review (D000078182). 'Umbrella Review' is an entry term of Systematic Review.

rapid-review.note: Evidence Synthesis (D000099290). No heading or entry term; nearest is Evidence Synthesis.

realist-review.note: Evidence Synthesis (D000099290). No heading or entry term; nearest is Evidence Synthesis.

reliability.note: Reproducibility of Results (D015203). Own heading ('Test-Retest Reliability' is an entry term), under Epidemiologic Research Design.

validation.note: Validation Study (D023361). Validation Study publication type.

nomological.note: Validation Study (D023361). No heading for nomological networks or construct validity; nearest is Validation Study.

analytical-model.note: Models, Theoretical (D008962). Own heading; 'Mathematical Model' is an entry term.

simulation.note: Computer Simulation (D003198). Own heading, under Computing Methodologies.

reasoning._about: An overlay, not a regrouping: the tree view can light up the Methods marked with one approach to theory development. The approaches and their definitions come from Saunders et al. (2019), section 4.5, which says outright that a study can combine them and that the choice depends on the topic and the researcher's philosophy, and which names no Methods. So each Method's mark has its own source (cite, url); basis named means that source names the reasoning, definition that we applied Saunders et al.'s Table 4.4 to how that source defines the Method (note says why). A Method with two or more groups goes either way. basis ours means no source we read settles it, so we assigned it ourselves by applying Table 4.4 to the Method's own definition on its card (note says why; the app shows it apart, as our reading). A Method left out is not marked.
reasoning.name: Saunders et al. (2019)
reasoning.cite: Saunders, Bristow, Thornhill & Lewis (2019). Understanding research philosophy and approaches to theory development. In Research Methods for Business Students, 8th edition, section 4.5, pp. 152–158. Pearson.
reasoning.rule: Not rigid: one study can combine deduction and induction, and the choice depends on the topic and the researcher's philosophy.

groups.name: Deductive
groups.def: Start from a theory and collect data to test the hypotheses it implies.

groups.name: Inductive
groups.def: Start from data, find themes and patterns, and build a theory or framework from them.

groups.name: Abductive
groups.def: Start from a surprising fact, propose the theory that would explain it, then test that theory with more data.

rct.note: Item 2b: hypotheses are pre-specified questions being tested.
rct.cite: Moher et al. (2010). CONSORT 2010 Explanation and Elaboration. BMJ.

ab-test.note: Section 1: the experiment retains or rejects the null hypothesis of no difference.
ab-test.cite: Kohavi, Henne & Sommerfield (2007). Practical guide to controlled experiments on the web. KDD.

nomological.note: The proposed interpretation generates specific testable hypotheses.
nomological.cite: Cronbach & Meehl (1955). Construct validity in psychological tests. Psychological Bulletin.

grounded-theory.note: Theory generated from data inductively; deduction and abduction also have a part as the theory develops.
grounded-theory.cite: Chun Tie, Birks & Francis (2019). Grounded theory research: a design framework for novice researchers. SAGE Open Medicine.

case-study.note: Findings can serve theory development and theory testing.
case-study.cite: Crowe et al. (2011). The case study approach. BMC Medical Research Methodology.

process-tracing.note: p. 824: evaluates prior hypotheses and discovers new ones.
process-tracing.cite: Collier (2011). Understanding Process Tracing. PS: Political Science & Politics.

interviews-thematic.note: p. 58: coding can be inductive, or deductive (theory-driven).
interviews-thematic.cite: Braun & Clarke (2012). Thematic analysis. APA Handbook of Research Methods in Psychology, vol. 2.

mixed-sequential.note: p. 17: mixed methods research uses induction, deduction and abduction. Said of mixed methods in general.
mixed-sequential.cite: Johnson & Onwuegbuzie (2004). Mixed Methods Research: A Research Paradigm Whose Time Has Come. Educational Researcher.

systematic-review.note: Reviews can generate or evaluate theories: theory building is inductive, theory testing deductive (Table 4.4).
systematic-review.cite: Page et al. (2021). The PRISMA 2020 statement. BMJ.

realist-review.note: Builds theory-based explanations, then tests and refines them in turn, as abduction does (Table 4.4); the source does not use the word.
realist-review.cite: Wong et al. (2013). RAMESES publication standards: realist syntheses. BMC Medicine.

design-science.note: An iterated build-and-evaluate loop in which theories are applied, tested, modified and extended, as abduction does (Table 4.4).
design-science.cite: Hevner et al. (2004). Design science in information systems research. MIS Quarterly.

case-report.note: Raises a signal or a hypothesis from a few cases, and cannot test it.

cross-sectional.note: Describes how common things are at one moment: patterns, not a test of a theory.

ecological.note: Compares aggregate data across groups to generate hypotheses.

surveillance.note: Repeated measurement to detect trends and signals in the data.

capture-recapture.note: Estimates a population's size from data; it tests no theory.

cohort-prospective.note: Can test a hypothesised exposure, or screen many exposures and outcomes for new hypotheses.

cohort-retrospective.note: Can test a hypothesised exposure, or screen recorded data for new hypotheses.

case-control.note: Compares the past exposures of cases and controls to test a suspected cause.

case-crossover.note: Tests whether a suspected trigger came just before the event.

target-trial.note: Writes the protocol of a trial first, then tests its question in observational data.

iv.note: Estimates the effect of a specified exposure, under stated assumptions about the instrument.

mendelian.note: Uses genetic variants to test a specified exposure–outcome relationship.

gwas.note: Scans millions of variants without a prior hypothesis; hits are new hypotheses.

case-cohort.note: Measures a chosen exposure to test its association with the outcome.

did.note: Tests whether a specified intervention changed the outcome.

rdd.note: Tests whether treatment at a known cutoff changed the outcome.

its.note: Tests for a change in level or slope after a dated intervention.

synthetic-control.note: Tests whether one unit's outcome departed from its synthetic twin after an intervention.

cluster-rct.note: A randomised trial: tests a stated effect of an intervention.

crossover.note: A randomised trial: tests a stated effect of an intervention.

factorial-doe.note: A controlled experiment: tests the effects of chosen factors and their interactions.

n-of-1.note: Randomised periods within one patient test which treatment works for them.

stepped-wedge.note: A randomised trial: tests a stated effect of an intervention.

adaptive-platform.note: Tests treatments against a shared control, and learns from the data as it accrues to drop or add arms.

field-experiment.note: Manipulates a factor with randomised replicates to test its effect.

ethnography.note: Understands practices and meanings from the inside, building concepts from what is observed.

delphi.note: Lets a consensus emerge from experts' repeated ratings.

scoping-review.note: Maps what research exists: concepts, methods and gaps.

network-meta.note: Combines trials to test and rank the effects of treatments.

ipd-meta.note: Reanalyses trials' raw data to test effects defined the same way everywhere.

umbrella-review.note: Like a systematic review: grades the evidence for claims, and maps a broad topic.

rapid-review.note: A streamlined systematic review, so it can go either way like one.

prior-art.note: Searches for what already exists; it tests no theory.

co-citation.note: Clusters emerge from citation data and map a field's foundations.

bibliographic-coupling.note: Clusters emerge from shared references and map research fronts.

multivocal-review.note: A systematic review with grey literature, so it can go either way like one.

diagnostic-accuracy.note: Tests how well a test finds a condition against a reference standard.

reliability.note: Tests whether repeated measurements agree well enough.

validation.note: Builds a scale from theory, tests it, and revises the scale and its theory in turn.

discrete-choice.note: Attributes and the choice model are fixed in advance and estimated from the choices.

interlab.note: Tests whether a measurement method gives the same result in different labs.

analytical-model.note: Derives what must be true if the premises hold: deduction in its purest form.

simulation.note: Works out the consequences of the mechanisms encoded in the model.

prediction-model.note: Develops a model from data, then tests it on new data.

economic-evaluation.note: Derives costs and outcomes of alternatives from a decision model's inputs.

pilot.note: Explores whether a study is feasible; it tests no effect and no theory.

think-aloud.note: Finds where and why users struggle from what they say and do.

pdsa.note: Each cycle tests a change, and its result shapes the next one.

benchmark.note: Compares methods under identical conditions to test which performs better.
